lesson.weeklyTitle: Introduction to Medical Informatics and the Healthcare Information Ecosystem

required.label: Acknowledge the module rules on patient information and AI (Part 5)
Submit at least one attempt of the formative quiz (Part 6)

blocks.html: This lesson introduces medical informatics by following a single laboratory test, from the moment it is ordered to the moment a doctor acts on the result.

blocks.title: This week's question
blocks.html: When an analyser produces a number, why is that not yet a reliable result in the doctor's hands?

Order → Collect → Transport → Receive → Analyse → Review → Report → Act

By the end of this week you should be able to

  • explain the role of medical informatics in supporting healthcare delivery and biomedical laboratory operations;
  • distinguish data, information and knowledge using biomedical or healthcare examples;
  • map the main stages through which a laboratory test request becomes a reported result;
  • identify key stakeholders, information hand-offs and potential information risks within a healthcare workflow.

This lesson has six parts (about 2 hours)

  1. Patient A's test — about 10 minutes
  2. What is medical informatics? — about 25 minutes
  3. The journey of a test — about 30 minutes
  4. Who does what in Singapore — about 20 minutes
  5. Looking after patient information — about 15 minutes
  6. Check and prepare — about 20 minutes

blocks.title: Fictional data
blocks.html: All patients, places, identifiers and results in this module are fictional.

blocks.title: Case card
blocks.html:
Patient A (fictional) is an adult with type 2 diabetes who attends an outpatient clinic at a fictional hospital.

At today's review, the doctor orders a renal panel (including potassium) and an HbA1c.
We will not interpret Patient A's results. This week we follow the information: who creates it, who checks it, and who needs it.
These three questions draw on your earlier laboratory modules. They are not marked; use them to see where you are starting from.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Medical informatics is the use of data, information and systems to support healthcare and laboratory work.

It is not the same as IT support.

A laboratory tracking specimens

Each tube is linked to its request, so the right result returns to the right patient.

A clinician viewing a result

The value arrives with its units, reference interval and comments, so it can be used safely.

A team reviewing a trend

A clinic looks at its HbA1c results over a year to see how well diabetes care is going.

blocks.title: Why this matters to a biomedical scientist
blocks.html: Your work produces laboratory results. Medical informatics is about making those results reliable, findable and safe to use once they leave the analyser.

Data — a recorded value without enough context to act on.
An analyser shows "5.8".
Information — data with context: whose, what test, units, when, reference interval.
"Potassium 5.8 mmol/L, Patient B (a fictional clinic patient), collected 08:40, reference interval 3.5–5.1 mmol/L."
Knowledge — understanding or rules used to decide what to do.
"Delayed separation of blood can falsely raise potassium, so specimens must reach the laboratory within a stated time."

blocks.title: The boundary depends on context
blocks.html: The same item can move between categories when context is added or lost. You will try this on the next screen.
Classify each example as data, information or knowledge. Then check your answers and read the feedback.

Before: data

"5.8"

No patient, test, unit or time.

After: information

"Potassium 5.8 mmol/L, Patient B, collected 08:40, reference interval 3.5–5.1 mmol/L"

Linked to a patient, a test, a unit and a time.

Context turns data into information. When context goes missing — a lost unit, a dropped comment, a result separated from its patient — information turns back into data. Weeks 3 and 4 return to this problem.

Data

Recorded values or identifiers without enough context to act on.

Information

Data placed in context — patient, test, units, time, reference — so it can be interpreted.

Knowledge

Evidence-based understanding or rules that guide what to do.

Medical informatics supports the whole chain: capturing data, keeping its context, and making it available to the people who use knowledge to act.

screens.title: From order to action: the journey of a test

blocks.html:
A laboratory test passes through ten stages. At each stage someone creates, checks or uses information.

  1. Test orderedDoctor
  2. Patient identified, specimen collectedPhlebotomist or nurse
  3. Specimen transportedPorter or courier
  4. Received and registered in the laboratoryLaboratory staff
  5. Prepared for analysisMedical technologist
  6. AnalysedMedical technologist with analyser
  7. Reviewed before releaseMedical technologist; senior or pathologist as required
  8. ReportedLaboratory
  9. Received by the doctorDoctor (or covering doctor)
  10. Acted on and communicatedDoctor; patient

blocks.title: Systems by role only
blocks.html: This week, information systems are named only by what they are for — for example, "where the order is placed" or "the system that manages laboratory work". Week 2 explains what these systems do.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html: A hand-off is any point where information or a specimen passes between people or places.

Hand-offs in Patient A's journey include:

  • doctor → phlebotomist or nurse (the order)
  • clinic → porter or courier (specimens and request)
  • courier → laboratory reception (specimens arrive)
  • reception → medical technologist (registered specimen)
  • analyser → reviewer (measured values for review)
  • laboratory → doctor (the report)
  • doctor → patient (the decision and what it means)

Hand-offs are where errors, delays and losses tend to happen, because responsibility and information both change hands.

screens.title: Worked example: from collection to laboratory receipt

blocks.html:
Follow one hand-off step by step: the specimen leaves the clinic and arrives in the laboratory.

  1. Created at collection: labelled tubes, the collection time and the identity of the person who collected the blood.
  2. What travels: the specimens together with the request.
  3. What the laboratory checks: the label matches the request, the specimen is suitable, and the time of receipt is recorded.
  4. What can go wrong: a wrong label (error) · late arrival (delay) · a missing collection time (loss).
  5. Consequence: a correct analysis on the wrong or unsuitable specimen still gives an unreliable result.

blocks.title: The key point
blocks.html: An analyser can work perfectly and still produce a result that should not be trusted, because reliability depends on every step before and after analysis.

screens.title: Your turn: the report reaches the doctor

blocks.html: Now annotate a different hand-off: the laboratory report → the doctor. Use the worked example as your model.

Error

The information is wrong — for example, a result attached to the wrong patient.

Delay

The right information arrives too late to support the decision.

Loss

The information is missing or never reaches anyone who can act on it.

blocks.title: In the practical
blocks.html: You will use these same symbols on your journey map. They differ by shape, so they can be told apart without colour.

Patient A's test happens inside a wider system. You only need to recognise these roles now; Week 9 looks at them in depth.

Ministry of Health (MOH)

Sets health policy and regulates healthcare services.

Synapxe

The national HealthTech agency for the public healthcare sector. It builds and runs national systems, including the NEHR and HealthHub. It is not a regulator.

Public healthcare clusters

Three regional clusters deliver public healthcare: NHG Health (Central), NUHS (Western) and SingHealth (Eastern). Each uses its own institutional systems.

NEHR

The National Electronic Health Record: a national repository of selected key health information copied from providers' own systems. It does not hold every record or doctors' detailed notes.

HealthHub

A patient-facing app for viewing records, booking appointments and paying bills. It is not the NEHR, although some records it shows come from the NEHR.

How they connect: MOH regulates · Synapxe builds and runs national systems · clusters and other providers deliver care · providers share key information with the NEHR · patients view some of it through HealthHub.

blocks.title: Looking ahead
blocks.html: Under the Health Information Act (passed in January 2026), licensed healthcare providers, including clinical laboratories, will be required to contribute key health information, such as laboratory results, to the NEHR. MOH intends the Act to take effect from early 2027. Weeks 4, 8 and 9 cover this.

blocks.title: Guiding question
blocks.html: What does the NEHR hold, what does it not hold, and who manages it?
Read the Synapxe page about the NEHR (about 8 minutes). It opens in a new tab.

items.text: Synapxe, About National Electronic Health Record System (NEHR).

blocks.title: If the link does not open: summary of the source
blocks.html:
• The NEHR is a national repository of selected key health information, copied from healthcare institutions' own systems. It does not hold doctors' detailed notes.
  • It is owned by MOH and managed by Synapxe, and has been in use since 2011.
  • Access is limited to authorised healthcare professionals who are providing care to the patient.
  • Patients can see which providers have accessed their record through HealthHub.

screens.title: Match each organisation to its role

blocks.html:
• MOH regulates; Synapxe builds and runs national systems; clusters deliver care.
  • The NEHR holds selected key health information — not every record.
  • HealthHub is a patient app — not the NEHR.
  • A hospital's own record system is separate from these national shared services.

Recognising these distinctions is enough for now. Week 9 returns to the Singapore ecosystem in depth.

Confidentiality

Only people who need the information for their role can see it.

Laboratory example: a result is visible only to staff involved in the patient's care.

Integrity

Information is accurate, complete and attached to the right patient.

Laboratory example: the value, its units and the patient it belongs to are all correct.

Availability

Information is there when it is needed.

Laboratory example: the doctor can see the result when deciding on care.

blocks.title: A common misunderstanding
blocks.html: Confidentiality does not mean that nobody sees the data. It means the right people see it.

screens.title: Module rules: patient information and AI

blocks.title: Three rules for this module
blocks.html:
1. Never enter identifiable patient information into external AI tools.
  2. This module uses fictional data and approved tools only.
  3. Never access the NEHR or any real patient record for coursework, including on placement.

The same care applies to confidential institutional information, unreleased research data, passwords and login details: none of these should be entered into public AI tools.

The NEHR may be used only for patient care and approved purposes. It is not available for teaching or coursework.

items.text: Ministry of Health, Circular MOH-MHC-0018-2026, Overview and Implementation of the Health Information Act (6 Mar 2026).

blocks.html:
• Confidentiality: the right people, and only them.
  • Integrity: accurate, complete and attached to the right patient.
  • Availability: there when it is needed.

Looking ahead: Week 2 adds who can access what in information systems; Week 8 covers governance and the law.

Practical: Map the journey of a laboratory test

This is Part 1 of a two-week task. You will keep your map and extend it in Week 2.

blocks.title: Case card
blocks.html:
Patient A (fictional) is an adult with type 2 diabetes attending the outpatient clinic at Riverside General Hospital (fictional). At today's review, the doctor orders a renal panel (including potassium) and an HbA1c. Blood is taken in the clinic and sent to the hospital laboratory. The results will return to the doctor, who will decide on follow-up.

You will not interpret Patient A's results. Your job is to follow the information.

Your role

Your role will be assigned in class: ordering doctor, phlebotomist or clinic nurse, medical technologist, or clinic administrator.

What you will produce

An information-journey map on an A3 template, in your group.

Success criteria

  1. Main stages from order to clinical use shown in sequence
  2. Each stage names who acts and the information created or used
  3. At least four hand-offs marked
  4. At least three risk points, classified with consequences
  5. Confidentiality and integrity points marked
  6. Privacy decision justified
  7. Explanation of why an analyser value alone is not reliable

blocks.title: Big idea
blocks.html: A laboratory result is the product of a chain of people, information and hand-offs. Its reliability depends on the whole chain, not only on the analyser.

Back to this week's question: an analyser value is not yet a reliable result because it must still be attached to the right patient, reviewed, reported with its context and received by the right doctor in time.

Next week: your map gains a systems layer — where information systems create, check and move information, and what happens when one fails.
